titel: REITs and other indirect real estate
kurz: How REITs, real estate funds and crowdfunding give you access to property without a deed, and how much they differ in liquidity, pricing, taxation and default risk.

bloecke.md: There are three ways to invest in real estate without your name on a deed: through a company or fund that owns buildings, through a company or fund that lends against buildings and through a stake in a single project bought on a crowdfunding platform. What they have in common is that the transaction costs of a direct purchase do not apply. When you buy a house, closing costs typically add 2% to 5% of the price, and selling it with an agent often costs another 5% or more in commissions and fees; both are lost immediately. Otherwise, the routes differ more than the common label suggests. A listed REIT is a stock with a daily price, a non-traded REIT or an interval fund limits how much money can leave, and a crowdfunding investment is often a junior claim on a single project.

## Listed REITs

A **REIT** (real estate investment trust) is a corporation or trust that pays no federal corporate income tax on the income it distributes, as long as it meets the requirements of 26 U.S.C. §§ 856 to 860. At least 75% of its assets must be real estate, mortgages, cash or government securities, and at least 75% of its gross income must come from rents, mortgage interest and gains on real property. It must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income, have at least 100 shareholders, and five or fewer individuals may not own more than half of its shares. Residential property is not excluded: REITs own apartments, single-family rental homes, offices, warehouses, data centers, cell towers, hospitals and much more. Equity REITs own buildings; mortgage REITs hold mortgages and mortgage-backed securities and behave more like leveraged bond portfolios.

Economically, listed REITs behave like other stocks, with daily prices, price swings and a pronounced sensitivity to interest rates. The value of a property portfolio depends heavily on the discount rate, and REITs finance part of their portfolio with debt. Two figures matter most in an analysis: the gap between the share price and the net asset value of the properties, and the debt ratio. With 50% debt, every change in the value of the portfolio affects equity twice as strongly, for gains and losses alike. REITs also report funds from operations (FFO), which adds real estate depreciation back to net income, because depreciation understates the earnings of buildings that often hold their value.

Real estate is already part of every broad US stock index; since 2016, it has been a separate sector in the standard sector classification. An additional REIT fund is therefore a deliberate overweight of one segment, not a new asset class.

## Non-traded REITs and interval funds

The US counterpart of the German open-ended real estate fund is the **non-traded REIT**, today mostly structured as a NAV REIT, and the real estate **interval fund**. Both sell shares continuously at a net asset value (NAV) that is based on appraisals, and both buy shares back only within limits. Non-traded NAV REITs typically repurchase at most 2% of NAV per month and 5% per quarter. If requests exceed the limit, they are filled pro rata, and the board can change or suspend the repurchase plan. Interval funds registered under the Investment Company Act must offer at fixed intervals of three, six or twelve months to repurchase between 5% and 25% of their shares (Rule 23c-3). Private REITs and private real estate funds, open only to accredited investors, are often even less liquid.

bloecke.md:
The reason for these limits is [[Maturity transformation|maturity transformation]]. An office building cannot be sold in three days, whereas a fund share promises liquidity. This works as long as not many investors want out at the same time. In December 2022, the largest non-traded REIT, Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT), began fulfilling only part of the repurchase requests after they exceeded its limits, and other non-traded REITs followed. Requests were filled pro rata for more than a year.

In addition, there is the pricing. The NAV is based on appraisals and models, not on market prices. Reported returns are therefore much smoother than those of listed REITs that own similar buildings, and they are regularly mistaken for low risk. The low volatility is a [[Valuation artefact|valuation artefact]]: when market conditions change, the NAV follows only with a delay. In 2022, listed REITs lost about a quarter of their value, while many non-traded REITs still reported gains.

Here, a return without visible swings is a consequence of the valuation method, not of stable property values. Investors who use non-traded REITs as a substitute for a savings account take on two characteristics they do not want: the money can be locked up exactly when they need it, and write-downs arrive late and in steps. Non-traded REITs have also historically charged substantial upfront and ongoing fees. Before buying, read the sections of the prospectus on fees, on the repurchase plan and on how the NAV is determined.

Unlike shares of a listed REIT, these shares generally cannot be sold on an exchange. A sale to a third party, where possible at all, usually happens at a steep discount to the NAV.

bloecke.titel: How US real estate securities developed
bloecke.unter: The dates are documented. For current figures on individual REITs, use their annual reports (Form 10-K) and not headlines.

ereignisse.text: The REIT provisions, signed into law by President Eisenhower, let small investors own income-producing real estate through a company that pays no corporate tax on distributed income.
The passive activity rules end the tax-shelter partnerships of the early 1980s. REITs may now operate and manage their properties themselves.
Highly leveraged REITs cut dividends, issue new shares at low prices and sell properties. Listed REIT prices fall far more than appraised values.
Real estate becomes the eleventh sector of the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS), separate from financials.
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act lets individuals deduct 20% of qualified REIT dividends.
Rising interest rates; listed REITs lose about a quarter of their value. Large non-traded REITs reach their repurchase limits and pay out pro rata.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act makes the 20% deduction for qualified REIT dividends permanent; it would otherwise have expired after 2025.

bloecke.md:
Listed REITs file annual reports on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q with the SEC. Non-traded REITs that are registered with the SEC file them as well, and all of them can be read free of charge in the SEC's EDGAR database. The important figures are occupancy, lease expirations, debt maturities and their interest rates, the debt ratio, FFO per share and, for non-traded REITs, the volume of repurchase requests and how the NAV is determined. Distributions that exceed FFO over longer periods are a warning sign, because they may be financed with borrowed money or with new investors' money.

Figures for individual REITs change quickly. Take them from the latest filing of the REIT in question and not from a ranking or a sales brochure.

## Taxation

REITs avoid corporate tax by distributing their income, so the tax falls on the shareholder, and REIT dividends are taxed less favorably than those of most other companies. Ordinary REIT dividends are generally not qualified dividends and are taxed at ordinary income rates. In return, individuals can deduct 20% of qualified REIT dividends under 26 U.S.C. § 199A if they have held the shares for more than 45 days; this lowers the top federal rate on them from 37% to 29.6%. Above a MAGI of $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly, the 3.8% net investment income tax comes on top.

Part of a distribution can be a capital gain distribution, taxed at long-term capital gains rates, or a return of capital, which is not taxed when paid but reduces your cost basis. Form 1099-DIV shows the split: box 1a ordinary dividends, box 5 the part eligible for the § 199A deduction, box 2a capital gain distributions and box 3 nondividend distributions.

bloecke.md:
You hold 100 shares of a REIT that pays $4.00 per share during the year, $400 in total. The REIT reports:

- Box 1a ordinary dividends: $260, all of it also in box 5 (section 199A dividends)
- Box 2a capital gain distributions: $40
- Box 3 nondividend distributions: $100

In the 24% bracket with a 15% capital gains rate:

- Ordinary dividends: $260 × 80% × 24% = $49.92
- Capital gain distribution: $40 × 15% = $6.00
- Return of capital: no tax now; your basis falls by $100

The federal tax is $55.92, or 14% of the distribution. The $100 return of capital is taxed later, as a capital gain when you sell. Once returns of capital have reduced your basis to zero, further ones are taxed as capital gains immediately. In an IRA or a 401(k), none of this matters, which is why REITs are often held in tax-advantaged accounts.

## Real estate crowdfunding

Online platforms offer stakes in single projects or in pools of loans. Legally, these are securities sold under exemptions from SEC registration. Under Regulation Crowdfunding, a company may raise up to $5 million in 12 months through a registered funding portal. Investors who are not accredited may invest across all such offerings in 12 months the greater of $2,500 or 5% of the greater of their annual income or net worth if either figure is below $124,000; if both are at least $124,000, the limit is 10% of the greater figure, at most $124,000. Under Regulation A Tier 2, offerings of up to $75 million are possible, and non-accredited investors may put in at most 10% of the greater of their income or net worth per offering, unless the shares are listed on an exchange. Many deals are open only to accredited investors, that is, to those with income above $200,000 ($300,000 jointly) in each of the last two years or a net worth above $1 million not counting their home.

The structures differ. A **debt deal** is a loan to the developer, often subordinated to the senior bank loan (mezzanine debt) or secured only by a junior lien. **Preferred equity** ranks between the debt and the sponsor's equity, and **common equity** carries the full upside and the full risk. Whatever the label, the crowd investor usually ranks behind the bank, which holds the first mortgage. There is no FDIC insurance, and SIPC does not protect against investment losses. If the project fails, the money can be lost entirely, and there is rarely a way to sell before maturity.

With a share, the possible gain has no upper limit. With a loan, the best outcome is the agreed interest and the worst is a total loss. Ten projects at 10% interest a year, with capital spread evenly, together earn 100% of one project's stake per year. Before taxes, they therefore make up for one total default only after a full year.

The tax treatment adds to the asymmetry. The interest is taxed at ordinary rates, while the loss on a defaulted loan is usually a nonbusiness bad debt and counts as a short-term capital loss. It offsets capital gains first and then at most $3,000 of ordinary income a year; the rest is carried forward. Platforms often issue no tax form for small amounts, and the Schedule K-1 for equity deals frequently arrives after the regular filing deadline, so you may need an extension.

bloecke.md:
## Limits of indirect investment

Three advantages of direct ownership cannot be replicated with indirect investments. The first is [[Leverage|leverage]] on fixed terms. A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage finances 80% or more of a house, and the lender cannot call the loan because prices fall, whereas a margin loan on REIT shares can lead to a margin call. The second is the tax toolkit. Depreciation on your own building, the passive loss allowance and the 1031 exchange are available only to owners of the property, not to shareholders of a REIT. The third is control over the property and the timing of a sale.

In return, everything that makes direct ownership expensive and inflexible falls away: closing costs, indivisibility, the concentration risk of a single address, repairs and dealing with tenants. With $20,000 to invest, the choice between a rental house and a fund does not arise; only the indirect route is possible. With $300,000, you choose between two packages. Direct ownership offers leverage and tax advantages and involves work; indirect investment offers diversification and liquidity without work.

Indirect real estate investments offer divisibility and [[Diversification|diversification]]; in return, you give up leverage and the landlord's tax advantages. Anyone who knows this trade-off can choose deliberately. A non-traded REIT is not a substitute for a savings account with a better yield.

mitnehmen: A REIT pays no corporate tax on distributed income and must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income; residential property is fully allowed, so REITs cover almost every type of US real estate.
Non-traded REITs and interval funds limit repurchases, typically to 2% of NAV per month and 5% per quarter or to 5-25% per repurchase offer, and can suspend them.
Their NAV is based on appraisals, so the smooth return path is a valuation artefact and not evidence of low risk.
Ordinary REIT dividends are taxed at ordinary rates with a 20% § 199A deduction, which makes REITs good candidates for an IRA or a 401(k).
Crowdfunding deals are usually loans or equity stakes that rank behind the bank, without FDIC or SIPC protection, with limited upside and the risk of a total loss.

begriffe.text: Real estate investment trust under 26 U.S.C. §§ 856 to 860: a company that invests mainly in real estate or mortgages, distributes at least 90% of its taxable income and pays no corporate tax on what it distributes. It can be listed, publicly registered but not traded, or private.

REIT whose shares are not listed on an exchange. It sells shares continuously at an appraisal-based NAV and buys them back only within limits, typically 2% of NAV per month and 5% per quarter; the board can suspend repurchases.

Closed-end fund that offers at fixed intervals of three, six or twelve months to repurchase 5% to 25% of its shares (Rule 23c-3). Real estate interval funds hold properties, REIT shares or real estate loans.

Earnings measure for REITs: net income plus real estate depreciation, minus gains from property sales. It shows the ongoing cash earnings better than net income; distributions that exceed FFO over longer periods are a warning sign.
Part of a distribution that is not paid out of earnings (Form 1099-DIV, box 3). It is not taxed when paid but reduces the cost basis, so it is taxed later as a capital gain.
